analysis.one_liner: Lets the FDA provisionally approve experimental 'fast track' drugs for sale after only early safety testing, before effectiveness is proven.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee on March 16 and 20, 2015, and died there.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a new pathway at the FDA: drugs already designated as "fast track" (aimed at serious conditions with unmet needs) could be sold to the public once they were shown "adequately safe" — meaning early-phase safety data, or four years of marketing approval in certain foreign countries — even before large trials prove the drug works. Patients would have to sign an informed-consent form acknowledging the drug is unproven, and the maker would have to keep running trials toward full approval. The FDA would be barred from demanding safety studies beyond those early phases. The bill died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with serious or terminal diseases who have exhausted approved treatments could legally access experimental drugs earlier, without joining a clinical trial or seeking compassionate-use exemptions. Drug makers with fast-track products would also benefit, because they could begin earning revenue years before full approval.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Terminally ill patients seeking experimental drugs

how_it_helps.text: It lets drug makers request FDA authorization to sell fast-track drugs after early safety testing, rather than after full trials proving effectiveness.

Before receiving the drug, patients must be told in writing that efficacy has not been proven and must sign informed consent acknowledging known and predictable risks, including possible death or disease progression.

Sponsors must keep running trials toward full approval, submit all promotional materials for review 30 days in advance, and the drug is subject to the same risk-management (REMS) requirements as fully approved drugs.

analysis.who_pays: Patients who take provisionally approved drugs bear the risk of unknown or unproven side effects, since the bill caps the safety evidence FDA can require. Patients who take an ineffective drug in place of an effective one also lose, and FDA loses some control over what evidence it can demand.
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients who take the unproven drugs

drawbacks.text: Drugs could be sold to the public after only Phase 1/Phase 2 safety testing, before any proof they actually work; patients could take ineffective drugs and forgo treatments that do work.
FDA is barred from requiring any safety studies beyond the early-phase Phase 1/Phase 2 standard, limiting the agency's ability to demand stronger evidence even for drugs that showed warning signs.
The bill adds the provisional-approval period on top of existing market exclusivity, potentially extending the span before generic competition for these drugs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — earlier legal access to promising experimental drugs for people running out of options — is real and meaningful for a small population. The cost is a genuine safety tradeoff: the bill caps the evidence FDA can require before sale, and adding provisional sales before effectiveness is proven could expose patients to ineffective or later-withdrawn drugs. It is a defensible idea for terminal illnesses, but it was never debated, so its design was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee, which never took it up, so it never reached a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: H.R. 1376 was introduced on March 16, 2015 and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Four days later it was referred to the subcommittee on Health, and no further action was ever recorded.
The bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion action before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The regulatory status quo held: FDA kept its full authority to require effectiveness trials before sale, and drug makers gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The FDA's full-approval status quo held

sides.party_line_note: The bill was too small a player to reveal a partisan pattern: two Republicans and one Democrat backed it, and no chamber ever voted on it.

industries.industry: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies with fast-track drugs
industries.note: The bill lets these companies start selling drugs years earlier, before effectiveness is proven, creating revenue during what would otherwise be the trial period. It also extends their market-exclusivity clock, so the earlier sales come on top of existing monopoly protections.
The bill strips the agency of discretion to require safety studies beyond early-phase testing for these drugs, reducing its control over what reaches the market and when.
